vignette: The concrete walls of the holding cell had never held a name, only a number scratched into the plaster. What Huy remembered most clearly was the systematic rhythm of the interrogations, the weight of boots pacing outside, and the sudden, unannounced seizures of physical force that left him gasping in the dark. There was no logical progression to the pain. One day it was prolonged standing, the next it was electric shocks, then sleep deprivation that blurred the hours into a single, suffocating stretch. He could never piece together which instrument was used when, or which day corresponded to which morning. The experience did not settle into a timeline. The memories felt like they belonged to someone else entirely. Sometimes, when he was washing dishes or sitting at his desk, a memory of the event would come to mind suddenly. The frightening footage played over and over in his head, sharp and unbroken, forcing his body to brace for an impact that had already passed. Over the years, that unspooling sequence began to shape his daily routines. He found himself retreating from conversations that drifted toward the future. Talking about next month or next year felt like laying a trap, so he stopped answering questions about his schedule. He stopped making promises. When his wife asked about vacations or how they would manage their savings, he would simply go quiet or leave the room. He told himself it was to keep the peace, but the silence accumulated into something heavy. The distance between them grew into a permanent fixture. He worked as an accountant, a profession that demanded meticulous attention to ledgers and predictable timelines. Yet, the moment he had to step outside his office to talk to a stranger about a new client's accounts, his breath would catch. He would watch the unfamiliar person approach, cataloging their posture and tone, waiting for a shift that never came but felt inevitable. He would deflect, redirect the conversation to paperwork, or quietly suggest they schedule another appointment for a later date. His partner noticed the withdrawal first, then the missed dinners, then the long stretches of him sitting in the dark staring at the television. The marriage frayed under the weight of unanswered plans and unspoken warnings. They parted ways, and the apartment felt emptier than before. Now, at his desk, Huy audits a client's quarterly expenses when a colleague's casual question about his summer plans triggers another sudden recall. He forces his attention back to the spreadsheet, but the numbers swim. He has come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, or what might trigger a shift in demeanor. He carries this certainty in his shoulders, a constant low-grade vigilance that makes even a friendly nod from a neighbor feel like a calculated assessment. What troubles him most is the conviction that he has permanently changed for the worse. He sometimes thinks about the guards, the bystanders, the authorities who looked away. He is certain that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that the outcome was never inevitable. He finally stepped into a clinician's office seeking relief from the unrelenting tension. He wonders, quietly, whether anyone can help him stop watching the door. He is most afraid of losing control again, yet he hopes, more than he expects, to find a way to look forward without bracing for impact.
